blocks.content: Diagnosing a probe failure starts with a question this course has already answered precisely: which probe failed, since liveness and readiness failures have genuinely different consequences.
1. Which Probe Failed Determines the Consequence
blocks.text: 1. Which Probe Failed Determines the Consequence

blocks.content: Exactly the distinction covered across the Liveness Probe and Readiness Probe topics, a liveness failure restarts the container, a readiness failure only removes it from Service Endpoints, knowing which one failed is the very first thing to establish.

blocks.alt: The same critical distinction covered in the Health Checks module, now applied to real diagnosis

blocks.content: A probe's timeoutSeconds, covered in the Health Check Strategies topic, set too aggressively can flag a genuinely healthy, just momentarily slower, response as a failure, worth checking whether the timeout itself is realistic before assuming the app is actually broken.

blocks.alt: A timeout too aggressive for a genuinely, legitimately slower real response

blocks.content: 3. Common Cause: a Bug in the Probe Endpoint Itself
blocks.text: 3. Common Cause: a Bug in the Probe Endpoint Itself

blocks.content: Sometimes the application is genuinely fine, but the specific health check endpoint it exposes has its own bug, a false failure that has nothing to do with the actual application health at all.

blocks.alt: A false alarm, the app itself is fine, the health endpoint's own logic is not

blocks.content: 4. Or: the Application Really Is Unhealthy
blocks.text: 4. Or: the Application Really Is Unhealthy

blocks.content: It is worth taking this possibility seriously too, sometimes the probe is doing exactly its job correctly, and the application genuinely is in a broken or stuck state, this is not always a false alarm to dismiss.

blocks.alt: Sometimes the probe is right, worth genuinely investigating, not just dismissing

blocks.content: Exactly as with every other symptom in this module, kubectl describe pod's Events section states precisely which probe failed, and often the specific reason, the fastest starting point before digging further.

blocks.alt: The same Events-first diagnostic pattern, applied here to probe failures specifically

blocks.content:
kubectl describe pod my-app
# Warning  Unhealthy  readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503

code.content:
kubectl describe pod my-app
# Warning  Unhealthy  readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503

codes.bash:
kubectl describe pod my-app
# Warning  Unhealthy  readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Establishing which probe failed, liveness or readiness, is the essential first step, since they have genuinely different, real consequences.
An overly aggressive timeout, a bug in the probe endpoint itself, or a genuinely unhealthy app are the three recurring causes, kubectl describe pod's Events section usually points at which.
